| [CLAIM-815](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-815.md) | The exponent 3/2 shared by critical branching cascades and first passage of a random walk comes from one identity, the hitting-time theorem: the chance of total size s, or of first passage at time t, is 1/s or 1/t times a local probability that falls as the inverse square root at balance, so 3/2 = 1 + 1/2 | Fills the gap left by A5 §3 of the exchange "Rich Get Richer Power Laws" (2026-11-20). A notes that critical branching and random-walk first passage share the exponent 3/2 and says this "is not entirely coincidental: the exploration of a branching tree can be represented using a random-walk-like process", without the step. The step is the hitting-time theorem (Otter, Dwass, Kemperman). Exploring the tree one node at a time, the queue is a walk with steps X − 1, and the cascade ends when it first reaches −1, so the total size is a first-passage time. The cycle lemma gives the factor 1/s, and the local central limit theorem gives s^(−1/2) at zero drift. Off balance, the same local probability decays exponentially, which gives the cutoff of [CASE-303](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-303.md). Checked with python3 -I. | [CLAIM-830](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-830.md) | The mean-field derivation of the Barabási–Albert power law is the age mechanism in logarithmic time, so what separates linear preferential attachment from Gibrat's lognormal growth is the continual entry of new units and not the proportionality of growth | Fills a gap in the exchange "Rich Get Richer Power Laws". A says that linear preferential attachment "involves proportional expected growth" (A3 §4), contrasts it with Gibrat growth, which gives a lognormal, and separately gives the age mechanism (A5 §6), but never connects the two. In logarithmic time a Barabási–Albert node grows as e^(a/2), where a = ln(t/t_i) is its log-age. Uniform births make a exponential with rate 1, so P(K ≥ k) = k^(−1/(1/2)) = k^(−2), which is Reed's s^(−λ/g). Proportional growth is common to both. Entry is what makes the Pareto: without it, linear attachment among fixed nodes is a Pólya urn with a near-exponential spread. Checked by simulation with python3 -I: log-ages have mean 1.000, the CCDF slope is −1.98, and the 100 largest hubs were all born in the first 1% of the growth.
